newsitem.title: GERMANY: Good demand seen for Germany's New Year Bund.
newsitem.headline: Good demand seen for Germany's New Year Bund.

text.p: Germany's traditional New Year Bund issue, the first new supply of 10-year government paper here since April, will see strong demand when a bank consortium meets on Tuesday to price the debt, analysts said on Monday.
The new Bund issue, which will almost certainly become the new benchmark bond, will likely carry a coupon around six percent with a price at 100, they said.
"This is the first new issue in some time and professional investors need the paper to play against futures," said Timo Klein, analyst at MMS International. "Investors need the liquidity."

The Bundesbank, as issuing agent for the debt, has already announced that up to 15 billion marks of 10-year debt would be issued this week, followed by a further 10 billion marks worth in the third 10 days of the month.
Analysts said the government normally prefers a coupon at, or slightly below the current yield of the outstanding benchmark Bund, now offering 5.97 percent.
If that price holds until the consortium meets on Tuesday, the coupon is likely to be priced at 6.00 percent, though it could be 5-7/8 percent.
The existing benchmark Bund carries a 6.25 percent coupon.

Analysts said they expect the government to sell the entire 15 billion mark first tranche, splitting the issue about evenly between the consortium, the amount to be sold at auction and a share taken by the Bundesbank.
The Bundesbank normally takes a share of Bund issues for its market maintenance operations.
"If the issue is as well-bid as is expected, the Bundesbank may only take a couple billion," said Holger Schmieding, economist at Merrill Lynch.
The consortium will decide the coupon and the share of the issue it will take. The Bund auction will take place on Wednesday at 1000 GMT and trading of the new issue will start on Monday, January 13.

Schmieding expected limited market impact when terms of the new Bund are announced on Tuesday morning after the consortium meeting ends. The gathering, which usually lasts around half an hour, is scheduled to start at 1030 GMT.
"This is a big issue. When the calendar was announced there was some negative impact," Klein said. "But it has been priced into the market by now."
Others, however, said the size of the supply, which was larger than expected, would continue to weigh on market thinking.
"The long end of the German yield curve should be under some pressure for a while longer yet," said Ian Ford, analyst at MCM YieldWatch in London. "This is a lot for the market to digest."
